hints: Start by sorting the four drawings using two simple visual tests - is a nucleus present or absent, and is the cell small or large with what nuclear shape.
One cell is much smaller than the white blood cells, has no nucleus and a pale biconcave shape - think about which cell carries haemoglobin.
The three nucleated cells are leucocytes - one has a small round nucleus with a large amount of cytoplasm around it, the other two are larger phagocytes.
Compare the two phagocytes - one has a large kidney-shaped nucleus, the other has a multi-lobed nucleus with granular cytoplasm - match these to monocyte and neutrophil.
walkthrough:
Spot the red blood cell**
The tiny dumb-bell shaped cell at top left has no nucleus. Mammalian erythrocytes lose their nucleus to pack in more haemoglobin, and are much smaller than leucocytes. That identifies the top left cell.

Spot the lymphocyte**
The small round cell at bottom right has a very large round nucleus filling most of the cell with only a thin rim of cytoplasm. That is the classic lymphocyte involved in immune responses, not a phagocyte.

Separate the two phagocytes**
The two larger cells both have irregular nuclei and are phagocytes. The top right cell has a large kidney-shaped / U-shaped nucleus with clear cytoplasm - a monocyte. The bottom left cell has a multi-lobed nucleus and granular cytoplasm - a neutrophil, also called a polymorphonuclear leucocyte.
Final answer: Top left: red blood cell / erythrocyte; top right: monocyte; bottom left: neutrophil; bottom right: lymphocyte.

hints: On Fig. 5.2 identify which curve shoots up sharply from near zero to about 15 kPa - that steep rise and fall is ventricular contraction and relaxation.

The bicuspid valve closes at the very start of ventricular systole, when ventricular pressure just rises above atrial pressure - look for the time where the ventricular curve lifts off the baseline near 0.1 s.
walkthrough:
Read the ventricular peak**
The solid line that rises from ~0 kPa at 0.1 s to a sharp peak and falls back to ~0 kPa at ~0.4 s is left ventricular pressure. Read across from its highest point to the y-axis. It peaks at about $15 \text{ kPa}$ at ~0.25-0.30 s. The higher sustained dashed line is aortic pressure.

Find valve closure time**
The bicuspid valve between left atrium and left ventricle closes when ventricle pressure exceeds atrium pressure as ventricular systole begins. That is the point where the ventricular curve starts its steep rise away from the low atrial curve, at about $0.1 \text{ s}$.
Final answer: Maximum left ventricular pressure = 15.0 kPa (15 - 15.2 accepted); bicuspid valve closes at 0.1 s (0.09 - 0.10 accepted).

hints: Remember COPD has two linked problems - narrowed airways and damaged air sacs - think how each would lower the amount of fresh air reaching the alveoli.
Think what chronic bronchitis does to the airway lining - inflammation and mucus - and what that does to the lumen diameter and ventilation.
Think what emphysema does to alveolar walls, elastic fibres and surface area - and how that reduces diffusion of oxygen into capillaries.
walkthrough:
Airways are obstructed**
In chronic bronchitis the lining of trachea, bronchi and bronchioles is inflamed and secretes excess mucus. This narrows or blocks the lumen, so ventilation is impaired and less air and oxygen can reach the alveoli.

Alveoli are destroyed**
In emphysema elastin and elastic fibres are lost so alveoli cannot recoil, and alveolar walls break down. Many small alveoli fuse into fewer large air sacs.

Link to low alveolar oxygen**
Larger sacs have a much reduced surface area to volume ratio for gas exchange. With poor ventilation plus less gas exchange surface, less oxygen diffuses from alveolar air to capillary blood, so partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli stays chronically low.

Final answer: Inflamed airways with excess mucus narrow the lumen, impairing ventilation so less air/oxygen reaches alveoli; emphysema destroys alveolar walls forming larger air sacs with reduced surface area and loss of elastic recoil, so less oxygen diffuses to capillaries, giving chronic alveolar hypoxia.

hints: Focus on what a capillary next to an alveolus normally does - exchange of which two gases in which directions.
If many of those capillaries are lost, think about the total quantity of each gas exchanged per minute and how the body tries to compensate by breathing.
walkthrough:
Less exchange surface for blood**
Loss of alveolar capillaries means less blood flows close to alveolar air. So less $O_2$ diffuses into red blood cells and is transported back to the heart, and less $CO_2$ diffuses out of blood to be exhaled.

Functional consequence**
Blood remains poorly oxygenated and high in $CO_2$. Chemoreceptors detect this and increase ventilation rate in an attempt to bring more oxygen to the remaining functional alveoli.
Final answer: Less $O_2$ is taken up into blood so blood is less oxygenated; less $CO_2$ is removed from blood / more $CO_2$ retained; ventilation / breathing rate increases to compensate.
